meta.theme: a choice that reverses itself while the reasons for it are being spoken aloud, explained neither as deliberation correcting an instinct nor as talk overriding one, but as a selection effect in the medium, since producing reasons composes a preference out of whatever will go into a sentence, which makes the standard advice to list one's reasons conditional on whether the choice will later have to be defended to somebody who was not there

meta.reviewer_notes: The opening scene is engineered so that both folk explanations fail on the same detail, that the choice moved while the list did not, and every distractor in the set is one of those explanations restored. The final paragraph concedes that the wordless preference may be worth nothing and then refuses the inference that the two preferences are therefore interchangeable, which is where the implication question is decided.

quality.adversarial_review: Q1's live rival is the option that hard-to-describe features are the ones that matter most, which the final paragraph refuses expressly by granting that the wordless business about the light may be worth nothing that can be argued with. Q2's rival is the option about increased confidence, which is the sort of finding that sounds supportive and bears on how a chooser feels rather than on which option is chosen, whereas the account is entirely about the second. Q3's rival is the option that she had no settled preference before she was asked, which the first paragraph contradicts by saying she had decided before she left the flat and that the second viewing was a courtesy. Q4's rival is the title about honest choosers and hidden motives, which the fourth paragraph rules out in two sentences by insisting that she concealed nothing and was not mistaken about what she liked. Q5's rival is the option about the light, which the passage attaches to no flat at all and which the first paragraph forecloses by refusing to say what had settled the matter.

paragraphs.text: She had decided on the first flat before she left it. Not decided in any formal way; she simply knew, the way one knows about a room, and the second viewing that afternoon was a courtesy to the agent. Over dinner a friend asked her why, and she began to answer, and the answering took some time. The rent was good: forty pounds under what she had budgeted. The commute was eleven minutes each way. There was a second bedroom, which she did not need now and might one day. She worked through the list with the mild pleasure of somebody finding that her instincts have reasons, and it was only when she had finished that her friend observed, meaning nothing at all by it, that the three were true of the other flat as well. She took the second flat. It had lost on none of the things she had named and won on none of them either. What had settled the matter for her in the first place she never said, and it is not necessary to know.

Two ready explanations are available and they cancel each other. The first is that she thought it through and that thinking corrected a first impression, which is what deliberation is for. The second is that she talked herself out of something she already knew, and should have kept faith with the feeling she walked in with. Both assume that the list was a report: that the preference existed, complete, and that saying it aloud either disclosed it accurately or damaged it. Neither survives the detail that her decision moved while every item on the list stayed exactly where it was.

Producing reasons is not reporting a preference. It is an act of composition, and what can be composed is limited by what will go into a sentence. Features differ enormously in how easily they can be said. Rent is a number. A commute is a number. The quality of the light at four in the afternoon in a room where she would spend four hours a day is not a number and has no ready phrase, and to say anything about it at all she would have had to invent something, in front of a friend, over dinner. When a person is asked for reasons, the sayable features are not merely mentioned first. They are weighted, because the list is now the thing she consults. The preference is rebuilt out of the materials the language handed her, and the rebuilt preference is the one she acts on.

This is not a story about honesty, and it is not quite a story about self-knowledge either. She concealed nothing. She was not mistaken about what she liked; she liked what she liked, and could have told you afterwards that the light had pleased her. The distortion has a different source, and the source is not in her. It is a selection effect in the medium, of the kind that makes a photograph of a valley a record of what a lens is good at. Language is superb at quantities, categories and comparisons, and poor at whatever has to be pointed to rather than named, so a preference pressed through it comes out tilted in the direction of its competence.

What follows is not that one should never explain a choice, which would be advice nobody could take. The advice that survives is conditional, and the condition concerns the future rather than the chooser. Where the thing chosen will later have to be defended to somebody who was not there, a committee, a court, a family, the articulable features are the ones that will do the defending, and a preference tilted towards them in advance is not distorted but prepared. Where nobody will ever ask, the tilt is a cost paid for nothing. A sceptic could fairly say more than that. None of this shows that the unspoken preference was the better one; the wordless business about the light may be worth precisely what it looks worth, which is nothing that can be argued with, and a person who acts on it will sometimes be acting on very little. What the concession does not license is the conclusion that it makes no difference which of the two preferences you end with. A preference you cannot defend is still a preference you have to live inside.

questions.target_mistake: converting the account of what articulation does into a claim that the inarticulate features are the valuable ones, which the closing concession denies
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the implication will attach a condition to the usual advice rather than reverse it, since the fifth paragraph refuses both the blanket ban and the romance of the unspoken.
questions.stem: Which of the following is most strongly implied by the passage?

options.A: The familiar advice to set down one's reasons before deciding should be given only with a condition attached.
options.B: A person who cannot say why she prefers something has not really formed a preference at all.
options.C: Decisions taken quickly are more reliable than decisions taken after deliberation.
options.D: The features a person finds it hard to describe are, as a rule, the ones that matter most to her in the end.

explanation.expert_notice: The fifth paragraph opens by refusing the blanket prohibition and then states what replaces it: the advice that survives is conditional, and the condition concerns the future rather than the chooser. Two cases follow, one where the tilt is preparation and one where it is a cost paid for nothing.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that structure at one remove. If listing reasons tilts a preference towards the sayable, and if the sayable features are exactly the ones that will be needed when a choice has to be defended to somebody who was not present, then the value of the exercise depends on whether that defence will ever be called for. The passage never tells the reader to stop explaining; it tells him when explaining costs something, which is a condition rather than a prohibition.
explanation.question_type_note: An implication question takes the author's claim one honest step. Where a passage ends by making advice conditional, the implication is the condition, not a reversal of the advice.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author writes that a piece of advice survives in a qualified form, look for the sentence naming what the qualification depends on. That sentence is the implication the question will be built from.

distractors.why_wrong: The fourth paragraph insists on the reverse: she was not mistaken about what she liked, she liked what she liked, and could have said afterwards that the light had pleased her. The difficulty is in the medium rather than in the existence of the preference.
distractors.seductive_element: An account in which words build preferences reads easily as one in which a preference without words is not yet a preference, and the step is made in a single clause.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the second of the two ready explanations, set out in the second paragraph so that it can be refused along with the first. Both are said to fail on the same detail, that the decision moved while every item on the list stayed where it was.
distractors.seductive_element: The scene does end with a reversal after talking, and the moral about trusting one's first feeling is the one such stories are usually told to support.

distractors.why_wrong: The final paragraph grants the opposite in its own words, saying that nothing here shows the unspoken preference was the better one and that the wordless business about the light may be worth nothing that can be argued with.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the passage spends a paragraph on a feature that cannot be said, and a reader who takes the attention paid to it for a valuation will arrive here.

questions.target_mistake: supporting a claim about how a chooser feels rather than the claim the passage makes, which is about which option is taken
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that a strengthener will show the effect disappearing when the options differ only in features that can be said, since that is what the mechanism requires.
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's account of what happened at the dinner?

options.A: People asked to explain a choice take longer over it, though they end up no more certain.
options.B: Asking for reasons changes a choice very little when the options differ only in describable features.
options.C: People are usually able to remember, a week afterwards, the reasons that they gave at the time for a choice.
options.D: People asked for reasons report markedly more confidence in whatever choice they finally make.

explanation.expert_notice: The account has one moving part. Articulation shifts weight towards the features that will go into a sentence, so the shift can only occur where the options differ in features that will not. If there is nothing unsayable at stake, the mechanism has nothing to move.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that prediction confirmed. A mechanism earns its keep by saying where its effect should be absent, and this is the case in which the passage's own explanation forecasts no effect at all; observing none is therefore support of the strongest kind available. It also distinguishes the author's account from both rejected explanations, since deliberation improving a judgement and talk overriding an instinct would both go on operating when every feature is easy to describe.
explanation.question_type_note: A strengthener props the step from evidence to conclusion. The best ones confirm a case where the proposed mechanism predicts nothing will happen, since rival explanations rarely predict the same absence.
explanation.reading_habit: Ask what the author's explanation forbids. Evidence that the forbidden thing does not occur supports him more than another instance of the thing he already described.

distractors.why_wrong: Duration and certainty are not the account's terms. The claim is about which flat gets taken, and a finding about how long the exercise lasts is consistent with the author's explanation, with deliberation correcting an instinct, and with talk damaging one.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like laboratory evidence about explaining choices, and readers accept the topic as a substitute for the claim.

distractors.why_wrong: Memory for reasons is never at issue. The passage's mechanism operates at the moment the list is being made, when the list becomes the thing the chooser consults, and nothing in it turns on what is recalled later.
distractors.seductive_element: Anything about reasons and later recollection feels relevant to an argument in which reasons are said to do something to a person.

distractors.why_wrong: Confidence is about how the chooser feels, and the account is about which option is chosen. A person could feel more certain and still take the flat the mechanism predicts, or take the other one, so the finding leaves the claim exactly where it was.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because it sounds supportive and is easy to imagine as a real result, and because the woman in the scene does work through her list with evident satisfaction.

questions.target_mistake: concluding that no preference existed before the list, when the first paragraph records a decision taken before she left the flat
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the answer will describe the preference she ended with rather than deny the one she began with.
questions.stem: It can be inferred that, on the author's account, the woman at the dinner

options.A: was concealing from her friend the real ground on which she had preferred the first flat
options.B: had no settled preference between the two flats before she was asked, though she thought she had
options.C: chose the flat that came out better on the features she had named aloud
options.D: ended with a preference assembled out of the features she could put into words

explanation.expert_notice: The third paragraph states the outcome in general terms, saying the preference is rebuilt out of the materials the language handed her and that the rebuilt preference is the one she acts on. The first paragraph supplies the particulars, since she had decided before she left the first flat and the second flat won on nothing she had named.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option applies the general statement to the case. Her first preference was formed in a room and included something she never articulated; the list contained only the features that would go into a sentence; and the choice she finally made corresponds to the list rather than to the room. Assembled out of the sayable is precisely the passage's own description of what she ended with.
explanation.question_type_note: An inference about a narrated person is settled by matching the passage's general mechanism to the details of the scene. Both halves have to fit.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage opens with a scene and then explains it, read the explanation back onto the scene sentence by sentence. Distractors are usually built from the scene without the explanation, or from the explanation pushed past the scene.

distractors.why_wrong: The fourth paragraph denies it in three words, saying she concealed nothing, and adds that she could have told you afterwards that the light had pleased her. What she lacked at dinner was a phrase, not a willingness.
distractors.seductive_element: She does leave something unsaid, and an unsaid ground in a story about explaining oneself invites the language of concealment.

distractors.why_wrong: The first sentence of the passage contradicts it. She had decided before she left the first flat, and the afternoon's second viewing was a courtesy, so a preference existed and was displaced rather than absent.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because an account in which a preference is rebuilt during a conversation sounds very like an account in which there was nothing there to begin with.

distractors.why_wrong: The first paragraph says the second flat had lost on none of the things she had named and won on none of them either. The mechanism does not require the chosen option to score better on the list; it requires the list to become what she consults.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the obvious way for a story about reasons changing a choice to end, and readers supply the arithmetic the scene deliberately withholds.

questions.target_mistake: titling the passage by the anecdote's most vivid detail or by one of the folk explanations it exists to refuse
questions.prediction_target: The learner should compress the passage first: putting a preference into words rebuilds it out of the parts that have words.
questions.stem: Which of the following would be the most appropriate title for the passage?

options.A: Why First Impressions Deserve More Respect Than They Get
options.B: The Honest Chooser and the Hidden Motive
options.C: What the Sayable Does to the Chosen
options.D: The Light at Four, and the Flat She Did Not Take

explanation.expert_notice: The argument is stated in the third paragraph and guarded in the fourth. Articulation composes rather than reports, the sayable features get weighted because the list becomes what the chooser consults, and the source of the tilt is the medium rather than any failing in the person.
explanation.correct_reasoning: A title is the main idea in a few words, and it must need every paragraph. The correct option names the mechanism and its object: what can be said does something to what is picked. The scene supplies the case, the second paragraph clears two rival readings out of the way, the fourth locates the cause in language, and the fifth says when the effect is worth paying for.
explanation.question_type_note: Title questions obey the same altitude rules as main idea. Reject any candidate that could survive if a whole paragraph were deleted.
explanation.reading_habit: Write your own title in six words before reading the options. Doing so makes it obvious when an attractive candidate is describing the anecdote rather than the argument.

distractors.why_wrong: This is one of the two ready explanations the second paragraph sets up and refuses, and the fifth refuses it again by granting that the unspoken preference may be worth nothing that can be argued with.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the moral such anecdotes usually carry, and the passage's scene has exactly the shape of a story told to defend the gut.

distractors.why_wrong: The fourth paragraph opens by ruling this out, saying the passage is not a story about honesty and not quite one about self-knowledge, and adding that she concealed nothing and was not mistaken about her own liking.
distractors.seductive_element: A woman who does not say the real reason sounds like a study in concealment, and the vocabulary of hidden motives is the readiest frame for such a scene.

distractors.why_wrong: The light is an illustration of a feature that has no ready phrase, introduced to show what falls out of a spoken list, and it is never attached to either flat. A title that assigns it to the flat she abandoned supplies the very comparison the scene takes care not to make.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the most memorable image in the piece and the one readers carry away, and unsayable things make attractive titles.

questions.target_mistake: supplying the comparison the scene withholds, by giving the chosen flat an advantage the passage never records
questions.stem: According to the passage, the second flat that the woman took

options.A: was neither better nor worse than the first on any of the features she had listed aloud
options.B: was cheaper by forty pounds and further from her work than the first
options.C: had the better light in the room where she expected to spend most of her time
options.D: was the one her friend had preferred from the beginning of the evening

explanation.expert_notice: The scene closes with two sentences written to forestall exactly this question. Her friend observes that the three named items were true of the other flat as well, and the narrator then says the second flat had lost on none of the things she had named and won on none of them either.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that sentence in other words. The detail is load-bearing rather than decorative, because it is what stops the episode from being an ordinary case of reasons revealing that the second flat was better: no item on the list favoured it. That is why both of the ready explanations in the following paragraph fail, and why an account of what articulation does is needed at all.
explanation.question_type_note: A detail question about a narrated scene is decided by the sentence that states the comparison. Nearby plausible facts are the decoys.
explanation.reading_habit: When a narrative refuses to tell you something, mark the refusal. An author who says a thing was never said has put a boundary round what any answer may assume.

distractors.why_wrong: The forty pounds is the margin against her budget and not against the other flat, and no comparison of distances is made anywhere. The option turns two absolute figures into a trade-off the scene expressly denies, since her friend points out that all three items were true of the other flat as well.
distractors.seductive_element: The numbers are the most concrete things in the paragraph and are remembered as a pair, without the thing they were measured against.

distractors.why_wrong: The light is introduced two paragraphs later as an example of a feature with no ready phrase, and it is attached to no flat at all. The scene says only that what had settled the matter was never said.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because readers assemble a story in which the first flat had the light and the list beat it, which is a coherent tale the passage takes care not to tell.

distractors.why_wrong: The friend does speak, and what she says is not a preference. She observes that the three named items were true of both flats, and the passage adds that she meant nothing at all by it, so the remark is evidence about the list rather than advocacy for either flat.
distractors.seductive_element: A choice that reverses itself immediately after somebody else speaks invites the assumption that the other person was pushing, which is the most familiar explanation of all.

vocabulary.passage_use: which is what deliberation is for
vocabulary.meaning_here: careful weighing of a decision before taking it

vocabulary.passage_use: It is an act of composition
vocabulary.meaning_here: putting something together out of available materials

vocabulary.passage_use: the articulable features are the ones that will do the defending
vocabulary.meaning_here: capable of being put into words

vocabulary.passage_use: comes out tilted in the direction of its competence
vocabulary.meaning_here: leaning to one side, weighted away from the centre

mentor.challenge: A woman changes her mind while listing the reasons for it, and none of the reasons favoured the flat she ended up taking. Hold on to that detail, because it is what kills both of the explanations you will reach for first.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: A woman who had already chosen the first flat takes the second after listing aloud the reasons for the first, although the second won on none of the listed features, and the explanation is neither that deliberation corrected an instinct nor that talk overrode one, but that producing reasons composes a preference out of whatever will go into a sentence, so that the sayable features get weighted, which makes the standard advice to list one's reasons worth following only where the choice will later have to be defended to somebody who was not present.
mentor.main_idea: Explaining a choice can change it. The usual accounts, that thinking corrected a hasty impression or that talk overrode a sound instinct, both treat the spoken list as a report of a preference. It is not a report; it is a construction, and it can only be built out of features that fit into sentences. Those features therefore gain weight, because the list becomes what the chooser consults. The tilt is a property of language rather than a failing in the person, and it is worth paying for only where the choice will later have to be justified to somebody else.
mentor.simple_explanation:
A woman looks at two flats. She decides on the first one before she even leaves it, the way you sometimes just know about a room. The second viewing that afternoon is only politeness to the agent.

That evening a friend asks her why she preferred it, and she starts listing reasons. The rent is good: forty pounds under what she had set aside. The journey to work is eleven minutes. There is a spare bedroom she does not need yet. She goes through it all quite happily, pleased that her instinct turns out to have reasons behind it. And when she has finished, her friend remarks, not meaning anything by it, that all three of those things are true of the other flat as well. She takes the other flat.

There are two obvious explanations, and the author says they cancel each other out. One is that she thought it through properly and thinking fixed a rushed first impression. The other is that she talked herself out of something she already knew and should have trusted her gut. Both assume the same thing: that the list was a report of what she wanted. But notice what actually happened. Her decision moved, and not one item on the list moved with it. So the list cannot have been a report of anything.

Here is the author's explanation. Giving reasons is not describing a preference; it is building one, and you can only build with the parts that fit into sentences. Some things go into sentences easily. Rent is a number. A journey time is a number. Other things do not. The quality of the light at four in the afternoon in a room where she would spend four hours a day is not a number and there is no ready phrase for it. To say anything about it at dinner she would have had to make something up.

So the features that can be said do not just get said first. They get more weight, because the list is now the thing she is looking at when she decides. Her preference gets rebuilt out of whatever language handed her, and the rebuilt one is the one she acts on. Once the list was the whole of the case, the one thing that had actually decided it was not in the case at all.

He is careful about what this is not. It is not about dishonesty: she hid nothing. It is not really about failing to know herself: she liked what she liked and could have told you later that the light had pleased her. The problem is not in her at all. It is in the medium, like a photograph of a valley being partly a record of what the lens is good at. Language is excellent at amounts and categories and comparisons and bad at anything you would have to point to. Anything squeezed through it comes out leaning towards what it handles well.

So what should you do? Not stop explaining yourself; nobody could follow that. The advice becomes conditional, and the condition is about the future, not about you. If the choice will one day have to be defended to someone who was not there, a committee, a court, a family, then the sayable features are exactly the ones that will do the defending, and leaning towards them in advance is preparation rather than damage. If nobody will ever ask, then you paid the cost for nothing.

And one last honesty. He does not claim the wordless preference was better. The unspoken business about the light may be worth exactly what it looks worth, which is nothing you could argue with, and somebody acting on it is sometimes acting on very little. But that does not mean the two preferences are interchangeable. A preference you cannot defend is still one you have to live inside.
mentor.why_difficult: The scene is constructed so that the two explanations everybody reaches for are both blocked by one easily skimmed fact, that the list she produced did not distinguish the flats at all, and readers who miss it spend the rest of the passage arguing with a claim the author is not making. The second difficulty is that the account sounds like a defence of intuition and is not: the final paragraph grants that the unspoken preference may be worth nothing. The third is that the advice at the end is conditional on a fact about the future rather than about the chooser, which is an unusual shape for practical advice and is easily flattened into never explain yourself.
mentor.author_intention: To take a small reversal at a dinner table and use it to show that putting a preference into words builds a new one, so that the reader stops asking whether talking helps or harms and starts asking whether this particular choice will ever have to be justified to anybody.

paragraph_journey.note: She had chosen the first flat, listed her reasons over dinner, and her friend pointed out that every item on the list was true of the other flat too. She took the other flat.
Thinking corrected her, or talk spoiled her instinct. Both assume the list reported a preference. The list did not move, and the decision did.
Reasons are composed, not reported, and only out of what fits in a sentence. Sayable features get weighted because the list is what she now consults.
Not dishonesty, not ignorance of herself. The tilt belongs to the medium, like a photograph recording what a lens is good at.
Worth it where the choice must later be defended to someone absent, a waste where nobody will ask. And no, the silent preference is not thereby the wiser one.

mentor.tone_progression: It opens as narrative, quiet and closely observed, turns analytic at the second paragraph and stays there while the mechanism is built, becomes precise and slightly cool as the cause is located outside the person, and ends practical and unconsoling, granting the sceptic his point and refusing to make the wordless preference romantic.
key_transitions: 'It had lost on none of the things she had named and won on none of them either.' (paragraph 1): the detail that makes both ordinary explanations impossible.
'Producing reasons is not reporting a preference.' (opening of paragraph 3): the passage's central claim, stated flatly.
'The advice that survives is conditional, and the condition concerns the future rather than the chooser.' (paragraph 5): the practical upshot arrives, in an unusual form.
mentor.misunderstanding: The commonest wrong model is that this is a defence of intuition against analysis, which the fifth paragraph refuses by granting that the silent preference may be worth nothing that can be argued with. The second wrong model is that the woman did not really know her own mind, or was hiding something, both of which the fourth paragraph denies in consecutive sentences. Both readings survive because the scene has the shape of a cautionary tale about overthinking, and readers finish the story they recognised rather than the one that was told.
mentor.traps_summary: This set offers a rejected folk explanation as the implication, evidence about confidence in place of evidence about choice, the absence of any preference in place of the replacement of one, the anecdote's most vivid image as the title, and a comparison the scene expressly withholds. Asking whether the passage states a thing or merely allows it answers four of the five.
mentor.reading_lesson: When a passage opens with a scene and then explains it, find the sentence in the scene that the explanation was built to account for, because that sentence is usually doing the work of eliminating the obvious readings and every distractor will be one of those readings restored. The companion habit is to watch how an author ends: advice made conditional on a fact about the world is not the same as advice reversed, and options that flatten a condition into a prohibition are the most attractive wrong answers such passages produce.
mentor.real_world: The same tilt operates wherever a judgement has to be written down: a hiring panel that ends up ranking candidates on what fits a scoring form, a grant committee choosing among proposals whose differences are partly untranslatable, a doctor recording the reasons for a referral, anyone justifying a house or a job or a person to a parent. In each case the useful question is whether the decision will later be examined by somebody who was not in the room.
mentor.takeaway: Say your reasons and you will get a preference made of the reasons you could say.
mentor.reflection_question: Which of your recent decisions will ever have to be defended to somebody who was not there, and which did you explain anyway?
